findings.title: Unauthenticated raw, non-graceful error exposure via /rest/user/security-question, /redirect and /api/Feedbacks/ (inconsistent error handling)
findings.analysis: Observation: An unauthenticated GET to /rest/user/security-question (no email parameter) returns HTTP 500 with a raw Sequelize WHERE error and a full Node/Express stack trace that includes internal source paths under /juice-shop/build/ (e.g. /juice-shop/build/routes/angular.js, /juice-shop/build/lib/insecurity.js). Corroborating triggers reproduce the same class: GET /redirect returns HTTP 500 TypeError 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading includes)' with stack; POST /api/Feedbacks/ (any body) returns HTTP 500 with a raw Sequelize WHERE error exposing the Captcha model internals. These raw error responses are neither sanitized nor consistently handled: benign unauthenticated routes on the same application (e.g. /rest/continue-code/apply/<code>, /rest/user/password-hash) return a graceful 'Error: Unexpected path' wrapper, while the vulnerable routes leak internal query structure and file/line references. Security relevance: excessive error detail aids attackers in fingerprinting the backend (Sequelize/SQLite), identifying parameters and model names, and locating injection entry points. Impact: information disclosure (Security Misconfiguration), consistent with errorHandlingChallenge (id=27).
findings.false_positive_check: Benign control routes on the same application return sanitized 'Unexpected path' 500s, proving these are not framework defaults: the raw Sequelize WHERE text and full stack appear only on the three triggers and differ from the graceful wrapper. The behaviors reproduce with independent fresh requests (captured 2026-10-05T07:13:55Z: 500/2946 B raw WHERE + stack; 500/2531 B TypeError + stack; 500/2310 B raw WHERE). The raw text drifts across calls on a volatile boot, so the claim targets the reproducible raw-error CLASS and the 500 status plus stack/SQL exposure, not literal text.

findings.title: Unauthenticated exposure of Prometheus observability telemetry via /metrics
findings.analysis: Observation: GET /metrics returns HTTP 200 text/plain (Prometheus wire format, version=0.0.4, ~26167 B) with no authorization. Content includes HTTP request counters (2XX/3XX/4XX/5XX), process_*, nodejs_* (event loop lag, heap, GC), juiceshop_version_info (v20.2.0), juiceshop_startup_duration_seconds, juiceshop_orders_placed_total, juiceshop_users_registered, and juiceshop_llm_* gauges (juiceshop_llm_input_tokens_total, juiceshop_llm_output_tokens_total, juiceshop_llm_tool_calls_total) plus juiceshop_challenges_solved and juiceshop_cheat_score. No secret/token/key/password lines are present in the output (secrets scan: 0 matches). Security relevance: unauthenticated observability exposure allows any caller to enumerate internal metrics, request-volume signals, and AI/LLM usage telemetry (exposedMetricsChallenge, id=97). Impact: information disclosure (Observability Failure).
findings.false_positive_check: The /metrics endpoint is genuinely unauthenticated: the same request with no Authorization header returns 200/26167 B, while protected routes (e.g. GET /api/SecurityAnswers/, GET /rest/user/me) return 401/400 with unauthorized wrappers. Response content is a valid Prometheus exposition with llm_* gauges confirmed present. Reproducible with an independent fresh request (captured 2026-10-05T07:13:55Z).

findings.title: Cleartext CAPTCHA answer returned by GET /rest/captcha (CAPTCHA bypass via answer leak)
findings.analysis: Observation: GET /rest/captcha returns HTTP 200 application/json containing the server-generated CAPTCHA expression AND its cleartext expected answer: {"captchaId":10,"captcha":"4*1-4","answer":"0"}. The answer is arithmetic-verifiable against the expression (4*1-4 = 0). The captchaId increments with each request, confirming the server tracks CAPTCHA state. Security relevance: the challenge response exposes the secret expected answer to any unauthenticated caller, defeating the CAPTCHA's purpose entirely (captchaBypassChallenge). Impact: broken anti-automation / authentication bypass support; the correct answer can be submitted wherever CAPTCHA verification exists.
findings.false_positive_check: The answer is not client-generated: it matches the expression verifiably (4*1-4=0) and the server-assigned captchaId increments across requests (stateful server behavior). The response is always 200/47 B JSON with the answer field present across independent fresh requests (captured 2026-10-05T07:13:55Z). Note: the POST /api/Feedbacks/ submission path rejects correct answers (401 'Wrong answer' / raw WHERE), so the verifiable vector in this mutation is the cleartext answer leak itself; the bypass-through-Feedbacks path is broken.

findings.title: Unauthenticated account enumeration and security-question disclosure via /rest/user/security-question?email=
findings.analysis: Observation: GET /rest/user/security-question?email=<email> returns an HTTP 200 application/json with the account's security question for existing configured accounts, while nonexistent/inexistent emails return an HTTP 200 with an empty body {} (2 B). Example: ?email=bjoern@owasp.org -> {"question":{"id":7,"question":"Name of your favorite pet?","createdAt":...}}; ?email=fake@nowhere.y -> {}. Security relevance: a deterministic account-existence differential via a publicly readable endpoint (securityQuestionChallenge-class enumeration). Impact: username/user enumeration, which enables targeted attacks (e.g., knowledge-based authentication, spam, credential stuffing prioritization).
findings.false_positive_check: Both branches return HTTP 200 with content-type application/json, so status alone is not the signal; the differential is in the response body shape (full question JSON with id/question/createdAt vs empty {}). Controls: an unauthenticated request with no email parameter returns a different 500 raw error (a separate error-exposure mechanism), confirming the query-param handler is what produces the differential. Verified with two independent requests (captured 2026-10-05T07:13:55Z: known=200/139 B question JSON; fake=200/2 B {}). The route is mutation-fragile across boots (500 in earlier activations) but holds 200 on this boot.

findings.title: Excessive data exposure: unauthenticated /rest/memories returns full user objects including password hashes and tokens
findings.analysis: Observation: GET /rest/memories returns HTTP 200 application/json with all memories, each embedding the FULL User object: email, 32-hex password hash, role (e.g. deluxe/admin), deluxeToken, totpSecret, lastLoginIp, profileImage, isActive. A sample record: {"UserId":13,"User":{"id":13,"username":"","email":"bjoern@owasp.org","password":"9283f1b2e9669749081963be0462e466","role":"deluxe","deluxeToken":"efe2f1599e2d93440d5243a1ffaf5a413b70cf3ac97156bd6fab9b5ddfcbe0e4","lastLoginIp":"","profileImage":"assets/public/images/uploads/13.jpg","totpSecret":""}}. Total 6183 B across 10 records. Security relevance: password hashes (MD5, 32-hex), TOTP secrets, and tokens are exposed to any unauthenticated caller (excessive-data-exposure / passwordHashLeak-class). Impact: password-hashing material and account-credential material exposure; the deluxeToken, however, is not a valid signed JWT (auth attempts fail with 'no header in signature' / 'Invalid signature'), so hijack value is limited to the hash/totpSecret exposure.
findings.false_positive_check: The exposure is not auth-gated: a bogus Bearer token returns a byte-identical 200/6183 B, while genuinely protected routes (basket, wallet, whoami) return 401 for the same request. The User object is embedded server-side in the response, not constructed client-side (same shape with and without the Authorization header). Verified with independent fresh requests (captured 2026-10-05T07:13:55Z: 200/6183 B, 10 records, full User objects).

findings.title: Unauthenticated write gap: POST /api/SecurityAnswers/ accepts writes without authorization while the read is gated
findings.analysis: Observation: POST /api/SecurityAnswers/ (empty body {}) from an unauthenticated client returns HTTP 201 with a server-assigned record id (e.g. 29) and UserId=null, SecurityQuestionId=null, answer=null: {"status":"success","data":{"id":29,"updatedAt":"2026-10-05T07:13:55.2xxZ","createdAt":"2026-10-05T07:13:55.2xxZ","UserId":null,"SecurityQuestionId":null,"answer":null}}. The parallel GET /api/SecurityAnswers/ is read-gated (401 'UnauthorizedError'). Security relevance: the write endpoint accepts unauthenticated mutations and binds them to no owner (UserId=null), while its read counterpart requires authorization — a write-open/read-gated authorization gap (mass-assignment / broken-access-control class). Impact: unauthenticated creation of security-answer records, data integrity violation, and potential confusion/abuse of the security-question/answer flow.
findings.false_positive_check: The write gap is a method-level authorization anomaly, not a benign endpoint: the parallel GET on the same route returns 401, proving authorization exists in this namespace and is simply missing on POST. The response body confirms the record was created with UserId=null. Reproducible with independent fresh requests (captured 2026-10-05T07:13:55Z: POST -> 201 id=29 UserId=null; GET -> 401). Note: on volatile boots the POST gate has fluctuated (201 in prior activations, 401 transiently in this session); the current boot presents the 201 unauth path.

findings.title: Unauthenticated PUT mass-assignment on /api/Products/{id} (missing write authorization)
findings.analysis: Observation: PUT /api/Products/{id} (e.g. /api/Products/1) with an unauthenticated client returns HTTP 200 'success' and echoes the modified entity in the response body, accepting arbitrary fields such as name/price (PUT {"name":"x","price":1} -> 200 {"status":"success","data":{"id":1,"name":"x","price":1,...}}). Security relevance: the PUT route accepts write mutations from any caller without verifying authorization, while POST and DELETE on the same route are gated (401 'No Authorization header was found'), indicating a method-level authorization gap specific to PUT (mass-assignment / broken-access-control class). Impact: unauthenticated modification of product catalog data (name, price, description).
findings.false_positive_check: The PUT accept-ance is a method-level anomaly, not framework default: parallel POST /api/Products/ returns 401 and DELETE returns 401 on the same route, proving the namespace enforces authorization and only PUT is missing it. The PUT response itself echoes the modification (200/235 B). Reproducible with independent fresh requests (captured 2026-10-05T07:13:55Z: PUT unauth -> 200 with modified entity). The write is accepted without authorization within the request itself. Because the underlying DB resets between requests on this volatile boot, cross-request persistence is not claimed; the finding concerns the unauth acceptance of the write within the request.
